entry.evidence: tests how reliant the location of such earthquakes is on closed-access data

steps.action: Pose the question of how far a small remote intracontinental earthquake can be located using only Open Access seismic and geodetic data, and how far routine locations depend on closed IMS data.
steps.quote: tests how reliant the location of such earthquakes is on closed-access data

steps.action: Take the routine catalogue epicentres, magnitudes and 95% confidence ellipses from IDC, ISC, NEIC, ISC-EHB and EMSC (Table 1).
steps.quote: Routine seismological catalogues determined the location

steps.action: Examine the waveforms at the only open far-regional station, GT.DBIC, in short- and long-period bands; only Pn is useful for location.
steps.quote: Only the Pn arrival is particularly useful for location purposes

steps.action: From the dominant Lg and surface waves at DBIC, hypothesize that the event was relatively shallow.
steps.quote: the hypothesis that the event is relatively shallow in order to explain the dominant Lg and surface waves

steps.action: Survey open teleseismic waveforms beyond the ISC bulletin stations and characterise the strongly asymmetric station coverage (Figure 2).
steps.quote: We have examined significant numbers of open waveforms at stations not included in the ISC bulletin

steps.action: Beamform open small-aperture arrays (MKAR, MMAI, BURAR) and run VESPA-type backazimuth and slowness scans to confirm that the arrivals are coherent and come from the expected direction.
steps.quote: allow us to confirm that each of the signals at the time of the predicted

steps.action: Find no unambiguous depth phases at arrays or 3-component stations, and note that most onsets are emergent.
steps.quote: We see no unmistakable depth phases

steps.action: Compare the published epicentres and ellipses, set aside the EMSC solution, and examine the TORD and KEST Pn arrival residuals across bulletins to explain the discrepancy of the ISC-EHB solution.
steps.quote: Only the NEIC, CTBT, and EMSC catalogs are truly independent.

steps.action: Relocate the event with Bayesloc MCMC from the NEIC and the ISC published arrival times to obtain epicentre clouds and 90/95/99% ellipses.
steps.quote: We use the Bayesloc program (Myers et al, 2007) which can solve for the locations of multiple seismic events simultaneously

steps.action: Vary the station set (all stations versus Open Access stations only) and the arrival set (NEIC versus ISC bulletin) and compare the spread of the epicentre clouds (Figure 4).
steps.quote: The inclusion of the closed access stations reduces the apparent spread somewhat

steps.action: Check that the Bayesloc clouds from the NEIC arrivals agree with the NEIC bulletin epicentre.
steps.quote: the Bayesloc epicenter clouds using the USGS/NEIC arrival estimates are consistent with the bulletin epicenter estimate

steps.action: Conclude that the seismic lateral uncertainty is at least 10 km, that ISC-EHB is an outlier with an optimistic ellipse, and that the uncertainty still meets CTBT On-Site-Inspection limits.
steps.quote: with the available seismic stations, there is a lateral uncertainty of at least 10 km in the epicentral estimates

steps.action: Process Sentinel-1 ascending-track interferograms spanning the earthquake with LiCSAR (multilooked to about 100 m, adaptively filtered) and assess coherence (Figure S2).
steps.quote: We use acquisitions that span the earthquake date

steps.action: Establish that a small circular displacement signal at about 19.6N, 10.6E appears in all coseismic interferograms and in none of the interferograms that do not span the event (Figures 5, 6).
steps.quote: is common to all interferograms that span the earthquake date

steps.action: Compute the expected deformation wavelength (1 to 5 km) for an mb 4.3 event from earthquake scaling relationships and find that the signal matches it.
steps.quote: following the established earthquake scaling relationships

steps.action: Stack three fully independent interferograms and band-pass them with a Butterworth filter (15 km to 500 m) to isolate a line-of-sight displacement of up to 6 mm (Figure 7).
steps.quote: The resulting stack shows a clear, coherent line-of-sight displacement of up to 6 mm.

steps.action: Argue against a pure strike-slip mechanism from the absence of a four-lobe pattern, inferring dip- or oblique-slip; the focal mechanism itself remains undetermined.
steps.quote: The lack of a clear four-lobe pattern of deformation argues against a pure strike-slip mechanism

steps.action: Infer a buried rupture with a shallow source (5 km or less) from the absence of phase discontinuities and from the fact that the signal is detectable at all, citing detectability studies.
steps.quote: suggesting that the rupture did not break the surface, and that the top of the fault rupture patch is buried

steps.action: Compare the geodetic shallow-depth inference with the seismic absence of separated depth phases and find them consistent.
steps.quote: consistent with the lack of any clearly separated depth phases in the seismic data

steps.action: Compare the catalogue and Bayesloc locations with the InSAR location: CTBT and ISC are consistent, NEIC is marginal, ISC-EHB lies about 15 km off and EMSC about 30 km off; discuss hypocentre versus rupture-extent differences.
steps.quote: only those from the CTBT and the initial ISC catalogue are consistent with the more precise location information

steps.action: Raise, without excluding it, the rival that aseismic deformation enhanced the signal, given a deformation wavelength longer than expected for the mb range.
steps.quote: we cannot rule out the possibility that the displacement seen is enhanced by some level of aseismic process

steps.action: Retain the claim that Open Access seismic plus InSAR data give a precise absolute location for this small event, and that restricting to Open Access arrivals markedly increases seismic location uncertainty.
steps.quote: demonstrates the potential for geodetic data to both supplement, and potentially calibrate, seismological earthquake location

end.claim: Combining Open Access seismological data with Sentinel-1 InSAR locates the 2017 Tenere earthquake to within one rupture length (5 km or less), compared with at least 10 km from seismology alone, and indicates a shallow source.

decisive_move.sentence: Establishing that the small displacement signal is present in every coseismic interferogram and absent from non-spanning ones is what turns InSAR into a location constraint; without it the claim rests on the 10 km or larger seismic uncertainty.

gates.evidence: The catalogue epicentre and origin date directed the InSAR acquisitions (pairs spanning the event), but no stated hypothesis directed the data collection. The InSAR signal could have been absent or located elsewhere, and non-spanning interferograms served as a null test (p. 12). Nothing was fixed in advance; the filter band and the stack choice were set during the analysis (p. 12).

imports.item: Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo inference (Bayesloc)

limits: No peer-review file was supplied, so there is no review sequence, although the acknowledgements thank two reviewers. The supplied text is the EarthArXiv preprint, not the typeset GJI version. The velocity model used in Bayesloc is not stated. The InSAR location uncertainty is argued from rupture length and visual assessment, not from a formal inversion; no fault model, slip or geodetic magnitude is estimated. Sub-claims and their statuses: seismic lateral uncertainty of at least 10 km (estimate_with_resolution); shallow source of 5 km or less (best_explanation, consistent with the absence of depth phases); dip- or oblique-slip rather than pure strike-slip (best_explanation, weak); rupture blanketed by unconsolidated sediment (best_explanation, speculative); aseismic contribution not excluded (none). Entry could also be read as challenged_result, since the paper assesses the validity of routine catalogue locations (p. 4); this is inference. The coherence characterisation (Figure S2) is reported only in the supplement, which was not supplied.
